A cumulative register's own guarantee (it only ever goes up) is exactly what makes a negative difference diagnostic rather than merely wrong — the direction of the anomaly tells you something broke, long before you know which of the three things it was.

at.step: Reveal: a register is cumulative, consumption is a difference

items.item: A rollover, a reset and a meter swap all look identical as a single negative number in a difference column — the three only separate once you bring in side information the raw numbers don't carry: the register's known width, a plausibility band, and install-history metadata.

at.step: Predict: does a negative difference always mean the same thing?

items.item: Correcting a rollover is not a heuristic, it's exact arithmetic, once the register's fixed width is known — there is zero uncertainty left in that correction, unlike the other two failure modes.

at.step: Reveal: a rollover, corrected for real

items.item: A bound is not a weaker answer than a point estimate — for a genuinely unobserved reset, a bound is the strongest true statement available, and presenting a point estimate anyway would be a stronger-sounding but false claim.

at.step: Reveal: a reset, bounded but never recovered

items.item: A system that silently replaces missing information with a confident default (zero) is more dangerous than one that visibly admits the gap, because the first produces numbers nobody has reason to double-check.

at.step: Reveal: the old fix was worse than an honest bound

items.item: A meter swap isn't a data-quality problem to detect and clean, it's a legitimate changeover that needs its own lifecycle event (an install record) feeding the pipeline, the same way topic 1's hierarchy needed a valid-time window rather than a lookup table.

at.step: Reveal: a meter swap, split rather than diffed

items.item: Treating a varying rate as if it were constant between samples is the single most common unit error in any metered system, and it is invisible in the arithmetic (an average times a duration looks exactly as valid as an integral) until you check it against the real sample spacing.

at.step: Reveal: power integrated into energy, against the naive average

items.item: An allocation rule is chosen, not measured, which means every KPI built on top of it (energy per unit, a sustainability figure) inherits that same chosen, not measured, quality — reporting the spread alongside the number is the only honest way to convey that.

at.step: Reveal: one header meter, two allocation rules, a costed spread

items.item: Converting an allocation spread into a currency figure (rather than leaving it as an abstract kWh range) is what makes the uncertainty legible to someone who has to decide whether it's worth resolving — an unquantified 'this number is a bit uncertain' rarely survives contact with a budget conversation.

at.step: Reveal: one header meter, two allocation rules, a costed spread

items.item: A sustainability or carbon-footprint figure that cites an energy-per-unit KPI without naming the allocation rule behind it is reporting a number with an invisible, unstated assumption baked in.

at.step: Prove it
